display.purpose: Ceremonial headings, login logo, pricing numbers, level titles. Always uppercase, always tracked.

label.purpose: The system's default UI voice — field labels, button text, nav labels, stat captions.

body.purpose: General copy, modal text, form values.

mono.purpose: Coordinate readouts and other machine-output data.

shadows.name: ambient-lg
shadows.purpose: Sidebar, drawers, login card, full modals.

shadows.name: drawer-sweep
shadows.purpose: Right-side slide-in panels (history, admin, map, subscription).

shadows.name: button-inset
shadows.purpose: Top-edge sheen on raised buttons, communicating pressability.

motion.name: ease-standard
motion.purpose: Default transition for sidebar collapse, nav state, focus/hover changes.

motion.name: btn-transition
motion.value: background .15s, color .15s, border-color .15s, box-shadow .15s, opacity .15s, filter .15s, transform .15s
motion.purpose: Shared transition property list for every button/icon-control; referenced via var(--btn-transition), never transition: all.

narrative.overview: Rota Manager is built for the cab of a delivery vehicle, not a desk. The system reads as rugged dispatch equipment first: a near-black navy base, hairline dividers, uppercase tracked labels, a repeating diagonal hazard stripe on the login card, and a mono readout for coordinates. It has to survive being glanced at one-handed, in motion, in direct sun. Layered on top of that industrial base is the product's actual differentiator: a pixel-art RPG leveling system (avatar, XP bar, badges, item drops) that turns the unglamorous work of correcting an address into visible, earned progress. The two layers don't compete — the terminal is the chassis, the game is the reward system riding inside it. This system explicitly rejects a childish or cartoonish game skin. The pixel art is deliberate craft, not a cutesy wrapper — it should read as earned insignia, closer to a field ribbon than a mascot. It also rejects generic corporate SaaS chrome; the amber hazard-stripe motif and mono coordinate readouts are the brand's own vocabulary.
keyCharacteristics: Dark navy field-terminal base, light theme available as a secondary mode, same tokens re-mapped
Amber (warning-tape) as the primary action and achievement color; electric indigo as the cooler secondary/active-state color
Oswald uppercase-tracked display type for anything ceremonial; Inter for everyday UI; JetBrains Mono for coordinates and data readouts
Flat tonal surfaces at rest; shadow appears only on modals, drawers, and interactive state changes
Pixel-art gamification components sit inside otherwise sharp, low-radius industrial chrome
Every animation respects prefers-reduced-motion; loading indicators slow down rather than disappear
Every interactive control resolves to a 44x44px touch target on mobile, even when the visual icon stays small

rules.name: The Hazard Stripe Rule
rules.body: Amber is the only color allowed to read as an alert-adjacent industrial signal. If a new decorative motif wants attention-grabbing, it's amber-based or it doesn't ship.

rules.name: The One Cool Voice Rule
rules.body: Electric indigo is the only cool accent in the system, marking selection/navigation state exclusively.

rules.name: The All-Caps Ceremony Rule
rules.body: Display and Label type are never sentence case. If a heading needs lowercase for readability, it belongs in Body instead.

rules.name: The Press-and-Release Rule
rules.body: Buttons carry an inset top highlight plus a drop shadow at rest, and both disappear on active/press. Depth communicates pressable, not important.

rules.name: The Reduced-Motion Floor Rule
rules.body: Every keyframe animation and transition goes near-instant under prefers-reduced-motion, except indicators whose job is signaling 'still working' (spinner, indeterminate progress bar), which slow down instead of vanishing.

dos: Do keep amber as the only achievement/attention signal — XP, primary actions, and the login hazard stripe all share one color language.
Do use the sharp 3px radius for anything interactive and reserve the looser 10-12px radius for passive containers.
Do default every new surface to flat + tonal layering; add a shadow only when the element temporarily floats.
Do treat the pixel-art gamification assets as earned insignia — crisp, pixelated, tiered by real accomplishment.
Do verify contrast for anything read outdoors: this app's baseline assumption is a driver squinting at a phone in sunlight.
Do scope every transition to the exact properties changing (background, color, border-color, box-shadow, opacity, filter, transform) — never transition: all.
Do hit a 44x44px touch target on every icon-only control, growing the box or the invisible hit area, never leaving a sub-40px tap target on a control a courier uses mid-route.
donts: Don't let gamification tip childish or cartoonish — no mascot faces, no bouncy/elastic easing, no candy-bright secondary palette.
Don't flatten this into a generic corporate SaaS dashboard — no gray-and-blue enterprise chrome, no default Material card grid.
Don't introduce a second cool accent color alongside Electric Indigo, and don't reuse it for anything other than navigation/selection state.
Don't add resting-state shadows to cards or panels — depth comes from the two-step navy tonal system, not drop shadows.
Don't use border-left/border-right colored stripes as a callout pattern — the one stripe motif is the diagonal hazard stripe on the login card specifically.
